name: The Picturesque Georgian

severity_by_style.why: A Georgian house composed picturesquely is not a defective Georgian; it is a different species.
A temple front cannot be assembled additively.
The revival is genuinely looser about massing than the original and always was - but not this loose.

symptom: A house detailed as Georgian or Colonial Revival - pedimented door surround, 6/6 sash, shutters, a dentil cornice - and assembled as a picturesque composition: a projecting entry gable, a bumped-out breakfast nook, a two-storey mass beside a one-and-a-half-storey mass, roofs of unequal ridge height meeting on the main block, and no single dominant volume anywhere.

cause.explanation: Plan efficiency and lot coverage drive the jogs, and design guidelines drive the rest: a great many municipal and HOA codes require 'articulation' or 'facade relief' in linear feet, and a bump-out is the cheapest way to deliver it. The elevation is then generated from the plan by extrusion, and nobody at any point draws the building as a set of masses. It is worth noticing that this fault is usually cost-NEGATIVE - every jog adds corner framing, flashing and a roof intersection - but it buys plan area, and area is what is priced.
cause.cost_saved: Usually none: $150-400 per jog in added framing and flashing. What it saves is plan efficiency and compliance with an articulation requirement.

rule_violated.statement: A Georgian house composed picturesquely is not a Georgian house with a defect; it is a different species. The regularity is a claim about the owner's mind.
Two roofs of unequal ridge height meeting on the main block.
12-36 in, the only permitted break in the front plane, and only on the centre bay.

correct_practice: Some styles have a compositional law that outranks their ornament, and this is what the composition_parti slot exists to say. Georgian's law is strict bilateral symmetry about a central entrance; one simple roof solid about one ridge, unbroken across the full length of the main block; and every departure from the front plane limited to a centre pavilion breaking forward 12 to 36 inches on the centre bay only. Two roofs of unequal ridge height meeting on the main block is forbidden outright. This is not a preference about taste: no quality of trim recovers a picturesquely composed Georgian, because the regularity is the content. Conversely the styles that WANT picturesque composition have their own law, and it is not 'anything': the masses must be of clearly unequal weight with one dominant, and adjacent roof planes must differ decisively rather than approximately.

fixes.right: Collapse the composition back to one dominant mass with subordinate wings, and take the parti from the style rather than from the plan.
fixes.cheap: Delete the bump-outs and take the area in depth. A 28 ft deep rectangle costs less per square foot than a 24 ft rectangle with three bump-outs, because jogs are where corners, flashing and roof intersections live. This fix pays for itself and improves the plan.
fixes.dishonest: Keeping the picturesque massing and adding more Georgian trim to compensate. Every added pediment makes the disagreement between the parti and the vocabulary more conspicuous.

test.note: From an oblique photograph. One ridge height is correct for a formal style; two or more with none dominant is a picturesque parti wearing formal trim.

secondary_tests.note: Does one volume contain more than about 60 per cent of the building? If not, the composition is additive whatever the trim says - and this test is what the picturesque styles pass and this failure mode does not.
The only permitted break in a Georgian front plane is a centre pavilion of 12-36 in, and it must be on the centre bay.
One, and central. Three bump-outs is the signature of a plan extruded into an elevation.

detection: From an oblique photograph, count the distinct ridge heights on the main block. One is correct for a formal style; two or more with none obviously dominant is a picturesque parti. Second check: does a single volume contain more than about 60 per cent of the building's visible mass? If not, the composition is additive whatever the trim says. Third: look at the front plane and measure the deepest projection - on a Georgian it should be on the centre bay and under 36 in.

exceptions.why: Irregular, freely composed massing unified entirely by the skin is the style's definition; the roof gathers the volume rather than the plan ordering it.
exceptions.bounds: The unification must be real: one continuous shingle field over every corner and storey line, and one roof plane not less than 40 per cent of the total roof area.

bounds_test.note: The unification must be real: one continuous shingle field over every corner and storey line, and one roof plane not less than 40 per cent of the total.

exceptions.why: The multiplication of masses and gables is the point.
exceptions.bounds: The masses must still be hierarchically unequal, with a dominant gable or tower; equal masses read as accident here too.

bounds_test.note: The masses must be hierarchically unequal, with a dominant gable or tower. Equal masses read as accident here too.

exceptions.why: Picturesque asymmetry is the declared symmetry class, with a principal cross-gable steeper than the main roof.
exceptions.bounds: The principal cross-gable must be steeper than the main roof, never shallower, and it must be the dominant event.

bounds_test.note: The principal cross-gable must be steeper than the main roof, never shallower, and it must be the dominant event.

exceptions.why: Roof planes meeting at different heights with ridges deliberately not aligning is a diagnostic tell.
exceptions.bounds: Adjacent roof planes must differ in height by not less than 2 ft 0 in. Small differences read as error in this style too - the irregularity has to be decisive.

bounds_test.note: Not less than 2 ft 0 in. Small differences read as error in this style too - the irregularity has to be decisive.

exceptions.why: Deliberate romantic irregularity is the whole idiom.
exceptions.bounds: It must be crafted irregularity - swept roofs, rolled eaves, modelled chimneys - not orthogonal bump-outs.

bounds_test.note: It must be crafted irregularity - swept roofs, rolled eaves, modelled chimneys - not orthogonal bump-outs.

exceptions.why: A round tower, a steep-roofed entrance mass and asymmetric wings are canonical.
exceptions.bounds: One dominant mass, usually the tower or the entrance pavilion.

bounds_test.note: One dominant mass, usually the tower or the entrance pavilion.

exceptions.why: Asymmetrical massing under broad arches and heavy stone is definitional.
exceptions.bounds: The masses must be weighted and hierarchical.

bounds_test.note: The masses must be weighted and hierarchical.

inverted_by.statement: A formal symmetrical parti is the fault. The volume must be irregular and freely composed, unified by the skin rather than by articulation.
Symmetry is the fault, and a cross-gable shallower than the main roof is a second one - the principal cross-gable must always be the steeper.
A single simple mass is the fault.
Aligned ridges are the fault; adjacent roof planes must differ in height by not less than 2 ft.

confused_with.difference: That fault is a specific relation between two masses. This one is the absence of any compositional law at all in a style that has a strict one.
That is a flat-elevation fault. This is a massing fault, and a house can be perfectly symmetrical in elevation while being additive in three dimensions.
